title: EC-Council CSA
summary: The Certified SOC Analyst (CSA) from EC-Council is an entry to intermediate certification for people who work, or want to work, on the front line of a security operations centre. A security operations centre is the team that watches alerts and responds to them around the clock. It sits above general information technology certifications and below advanced incident response or forensics credentials, and it suits help desk and network staff moving into security, plus new analysts who need a structured foundation. It proves to an employer that you can triage an alert, gather the right evidence, use a ticket and escalation process and hand a case on without losing the detail. The exam is multiple choice and scenario driven, so most questions describe a situation and ask for the best next action rather than a definition. The domains below follow the published blueprint in order; because EC-Council has revised this exam more than once, confirm the current domain list and weighting with the vendor before you book. It leads to roles such as security operations analyst, tier one and tier two analyst and junior incident responder. This is an independent study guide and is not official EC-Council material.

beginner.definition: The Certified SOC Analyst is a security certificate from EC-Council. It is aimed at the analysts who watch for attacks and react to them. A security operations centre is the room or team where that watching happens. This certificate checks that you can do that job in a careful, repeatable way.
beginner.whyItMatters: Every large company needs people to monitor its systems day and night. This certificate shows that you already understand the analyst workflow. It helps you move from a support desk role into a security team. It also gives you a base for the more advanced investigation and threat hunting certificates later.
howItWorks: Learn the basics of networks, operating systems and common attacks before you start.
Study the published CSA blueprint and note every task listed under each domain.
Learn how a security operations centre is organised and how alerts move from queue to closure.
Practise with a monitoring platform so you can read logs and build a simple detection rule.
Train on incident handling, including how to write a clear ticket and when to escalate.
The exam is multiple choice with scenario questions, so practise choosing the best next action.
beginner.example: Imagine a quiet night shift when one alert appears. One user account failed to log in forty times in two minutes. Then it succeeded once from another country. A weak analyst closes it as a forgotten password. A good analyst asks three questions. Does the account have administrative rights? Was anything downloaded afterwards? Did other accounts from the same address try the same trick? The CSA exam tests that second kind of thinking.
takeaways: Learn the process as well as the tools, because exam questions test how you respond.
Understand the difference between an event, an alert and a confirmed incident.
Write clearly and early. Good notes make escalation and handover possible.

objectives: Explain how a security operations centre is organised and how analysts work in shifts
Triage alerts and decide which ones need investigation and which are noise
Collect and interpret logs and evidence from common security tools
Follow an incident handling process from detection through containment and closure
Use threat intelligence to add context to a security event
Support vulnerability assessment and reporting duties for the security team

chapters.title: Security operations and management
objectives: Describe the purpose, structure and shift patterns of a security operations centre
Explain the duties of a tier one, tier two and tier three analyst
Apply an escalation path and a service level so alerts are handled on time
Handle a security ticket from opening to closure with clear records
Protect evidence and follow confidentiality rules while handling a case

chapters.title: Incident detection and response
objectives: Explain the phases of incident handling from preparation to lessons learned
Triage an alert and set its priority using impact and confidence
Contain a live incident without destroying the evidence you need
Recognise common attack patterns such as phishing, malware and account abuse
Support recovery and record the lessons that should change future detection

chapters.title: Threat intelligence and hunting
objectives: Explain the difference between data, information, intelligence and threat hunting
Use indicators of compromise carefully and explain why they age quickly
Describe the main threat actor types and what each one usually wants
Turn a threat report into a detection idea you can test in your own environment
Join a structured hunt by forming a hypothesis and proving or disproving it

chapters.title: Log management and analysis
objectives: Identify the log sources that matter most, including endpoints, servers and network devices
Read and interpret logs from Windows, Linux and network equipment
Explain how a security information and event management platform collects and correlates events
Build a simple correlation rule and reduce false positives in it
Use time synchronisation and source context to build an accurate timeline

chapters.title: Vulnerability assessment and management
objectives: Explain the difference between a vulnerability, a threat and a risk
Describe how a vulnerability scan works and what it can miss
Read a scan report and rank findings by severity and business impact
Track a finding through remediation and verify that it is really fixed
Explain why scanning requires written permission and careful timing
